slides.title: What CORS is for
slides.summary: CORS lets a server say which other origins may read its responses. It relaxes the same-origin policy; it doesn't add protection.
body: By default, the same-origin policy stops app.example.com from reading a fetch response from api.example.com. CORS lets the API opt in with response headers.

ul: The browser sends an Origin header with the request.
If it matches, the browser hands the response to your JavaScript. If not, the request may still have reached the server, but your code can't read the result.

body: <mark>CORS is enforced by the browser to protect users. It doesn't protect your API from curl, scripts or other servers.</mark>

rows.head: GET, HEAD or form-style POST with simple headers

cells.text: Sends it, then checks the response headers

rows.head: PUT / DELETE / PATCH, JSON body, custom headers

cells.text: Needs an exact origin and Allow-Credentials: true

slides.title: Preflight requests
slides.summary: For non-simple requests, the browser asks permission with OPTIONS before sending the real request.
body: A preflight is an OPTIONS request describing the real one. The server answers with what it allows, and the browser only sends the real request if it fits.
Access-Control-Max-Age lets the browser cache the answer, saving a round trip on later requests.

body.note: If a request works in curl or Postman but fails in the browser with a CORS error, look at the preflight response in DevTools first.

steps.caption: The browser asks before sending a PUT with JSON.
The API approves this origin and method.
Now the actual request goes out, and its response is readable.

slides.title: CORS mistakes
slides.summary: Reflecting any origin with credentials hands your users' data to every website.

ul: Reflecting the Origin header back with Allow-Credentials: true lets any site read logged-in users' data. Check against an allowlist.
Allowing null: sandboxed iframes and local files send Origin: null, so attackers can too.
Forgetting Vary: Origin when the header changes per origin, so caches serve the wrong one.

body: <mark>Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * is fine for truly public data, and browsers never send cookies with it.</mark>

body.text: No. A simple cross-origin POST is still sent; CORS only hides the response. See the next chapter.
